text: Get set, posture, hands and your first music. Sit well, shape your hands, play with arm weight, and make music on the black keys from day one.

Let's get set before we play. Sit on the front half of the bench, in the middle of the piano. Your arms are level with the keys and your feet are flat on the floor. Shoulders down, sit tall, and breathe.
Let your arms hang down loose. Now lift your hands up to the keys, but keep that same soft shape. Round fingers, like holding a ball. That is your piano hand.

Put your thumb behind your middle finger to help it. Now let your whole arm drop into a black key, like a heavy feather, then float back up. Drop, and let go. The sound comes from weight, not from pushing.
Black keys sound nice in any order, so you can make music already! Low keys sound like a big bear. High keys sound like a little bird. Play low, then high, and listen.
Drop and release. Finger 3 supported by the thumb drops arm weight into the two black keys, each hand in turn. Press start when you are ready.
Way down low, way up high. Two black keys low with the left hand, then high with the right. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Velvet Market March. The band plays each phrase; you answer with your notes at the end of the bar. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Silver Carousel Rag. The band plays; you play your notes on the strong beats. Press start when you are ready.
Meet the keyboard and middle C. Find the black-key groups, then locate and play middle C with right-hand thumb.

Before we play, let's sit nicely. Sit in the middle of the piano, with your arms level with the keys. Make your fingers round, like you are holding a little ball. If your hands feel tight, shake them out and try again.
Look at the black keys. They come in little groups, two together, then three together, again and again. This pattern is like a map. It helps you find any key on the piano.
Find a group of two black keys. The white key just to the left of them is called C. The C in the middle of the piano is called middle C. It is our home base. Listen.
Every finger has a number. Your thumb is one, then two, three, four, and your little finger is five. Now put your right thumb on middle C and let it sink gently into the key.
Going to the right makes the sound go higher, like a bird. Going to the left makes it lower, like a bear. Listen, low, middle, high.
Play middle C four times. Locate middle C reliably and play it with right hand finger 1. Press start when you are ready.
Low, middle, high C. Find C in three octaves. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Velvet Garden Dance. The band plays each phrase; you answer with your notes at the end of the bar. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Copper Market Lullaby. The band plays; you play your notes on the strong beats. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Sunny River Blues. The band plays each phrase; you answer with your notes at the end of the bar. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Wandering Lighthouse Song. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
The musical alphabet, C D E F G. Learn the white-key names and play C to G with fingers 1 to 5.
Music only uses seven letters, A, B, C, D, E, F, G. Then they start again. From C we go C, D, E, F, G, A, B, and then C again.
Here are some easy landmarks. D sits between the two black keys. E is just to the right of them. F is just to the left of the three black keys. G is next to F.
Put your right thumb on middle C. Let your other fingers rest on D, E, F and G, one finger on each key. This is called C position. Listen to it go up and down.
C position up and down. Play C D E F G F E D C with fingers 1-2-3-4-5-4-3-2-1. Press start when you are ready.
Find the letters. Play named notes in mixed order without key labels. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Silver Teapot Dance. The band plays; you play your notes on the strong beats. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Misty Train Blues. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Paper Fox Rag. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Black keys, sharps. Name and play the black keys as sharps.
A sharp means one key higher, to the right. The black key just right of C is called C sharp. The black key just right of F is F sharp.
In the group of two black keys we have C sharp and D sharp. In the group of three we have F sharp, G sharp and A sharp.
Two-group and three-group. Play C sharp D sharp then F sharp G sharp A sharp. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Midnight Comet Rag. The band plays each phrase; you answer with your notes at the end of the bar. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Rainy Train Dance. The band plays; you play your notes on the strong beats. Press start when you are ready.
Feel the pulse. Play steady quarter notes with the metronome.
Music has a steady beat, like your heartbeat. You will hear four clicks to get ready. Then play middle C right on each click. Tick, tick, tick, tick.
This note, with a filled-in head and a stick, is a quarter note. It lasts one beat. Count out loud, one, two, three, four.
Four steady Cs. Play four quarter-note Cs in time at 60 beats per minute. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Paper River March. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Midnight River Song. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Reading the treble staff. Read C to G on the treble staff without labels.
Music is written on five lines, called the staff. The higher a note sits, the higher it sounds. This curly sign is the treble clef. It shows us where G lives.
Middle C sits on its own little line under the staff. Each step up on the staff is the next white key to the right, C, D, E, F, G. Line, space, line, space.
Read and play. Read notes from the staff and play them. Key labels are hidden. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Copper Harbor Lullaby. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Jolly Fox Tune. The band plays; you play your notes on the strong beats. Press start when you are ready.
Note values, half and whole notes. Hold notes for 1, 2 and 4 beats.
Some notes last longer. A half note is hollow with a stick, and lasts two beats. A whole note is hollow with no stick, and lasts four beats. Keep the key down while you count.
Listen to the difference, C for one beat, D for two beats, and E for four beats.
Quarter, half, whole. Play with correct onsets and hold each note for its full value. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Wandering Meadow Rag. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Velvet Parade March. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Count out loud, ta, ta-a and tempo words. Say rhythms as you play them, and learn the words that tell you how fast to go.
Rhythms have words. Say ta for one beat. Ta-a for two beats. Ta-a-a for three, and ta-a-a-a for four. A rest is a quiet sh. Say the words and your hands will follow.
Count the numbers too, one, two, three, four, in every bar. Clap and say the rhythm words while you count. When they line up, your rhythm is right.
Some words tell you how fast to play. They are Italian. Adagio is slow. Andante is walking speed. Allegro is quick and happy. Presto is super fast.
Say the rhythm. Hear four beats and pick the syllables that match. Listen, then answer.
Play and say it. Play while saying ta ta ta-a, ta-a ta-a, ta sh ta sh, ta-a-a-a. Press start when you are ready.
Name the tempo. Listen to the speed and pick the tempo word. Listen, then answer.
Play along, Lucky River Tune. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Velvet Comet Song. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Bass clef and the left hand. Left-hand C position, C to G in bass clef.
Low notes are written on the bass staff. Its sign has two dots, and they hug the line called F. Your left hand usually plays these low notes.
Now the left hand. Put your little finger, number five, on the C below middle C. The other fingers rest on D, E, F and G. Your thumb ends up on G.
left hand C position. Play C D E F G F E D C with left hand fingers 5-4-3-2-1-2-3-4-5. Press start when you are ready.
Read the bass staff. Mixed bass notes, labels hidden. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Sleepy Kite Blues. The band plays; you play your notes on the strong beats. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Wandering Kite Blues. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Wandering River March. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Landmark notes, read by steps and skips. Three notes you know at a glance, and how to read everything else from them.
Learn three landmark notes. Treble G, the treble clef curls around its line. Bass F, the bass clef's two dots sit on either side of its line. Middle C, on its own little line between the staves.
A step goes from a line to the very next space, or a space to the next line. On the piano, that's the very next white key. One step up from G is A.
A skip goes from a line to the next line, jumping over one key. One skip up from G is B. Look which way the notes go and how far, and your finger will find it.
Name it from the landmark, treble. Notes near treble G. Listen, then answer.
Name it from the landmark, bass. Notes near bass F. Listen, then answer.
The whole staff. Any note on the treble or bass staff, plus ledger lines. Listen, then answer.
Steps and skips from G. No letters on the keys, read each move from the note before. Press start when you are ready.
Steps and skips from F. Left hand, reading from bass F. Press start when you are ready.
First melody, Ode to Joy. Beethoven's theme in C position, first slowly, then in time.
Here is your first real tune! It is called Ode to Joy, by Beethoven. It only uses C position, and the notes mostly move to the key right next door. Listen and follow along.
Notes first wait mode. Learn both phrases without time pressure. Press start when you are ready.
Performance in time. Perform both phrases in time at 72 beats per minute. 80% to pass. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Silver Fox Tune. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Misty Lantern Dance. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Two notes at once and your first chords. Play intervals and the C, F and G major chords. The app hears every note of the chord.
Now let's press two keys at the same time, so they make one sound together. Try C and E. Then try C and G. Press them exactly together.
Add one more note in the middle, C, E and G together. That is a chord, the C major chord. It sounds happy and settled, like home. Use fingers one, three and five.
The same hand shape works in other places. Here is F major, and here is G major. Listen to C, then F, then G, and back home to C.
The app listens for every note in the chord. If one is missing, it will tell you which one. Listen to how full it sounds when the left hand adds a low C.
Intervals, two notes at once. Play each pair together. Press start when you are ready.
C, F and G chords. Play every note of each chord together. Press start when you are ready.
Chords in time. Change chords on the beat at 60 beats per minute. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Little Bridge Dance. The band plays the tune; you play the chords. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Misty Train Rag. The band plays the tune; you play the chords. Press start when you are ready.
Right hand, finger independence. Skip and step patterns that train each finger to move on its own while the others stay relaxed.
Keep your hand quiet and still, and let only one finger move at a time. The other fingers just rest on their keys. If a finger tags along by itself, slow down. That is what we are training.
Lift each finger from the big knuckle, where your finger joins your hand. Keep the fingertip firm. Try to make every note equally loud.
Skips, 1-3, 2-4, 3-5. Play the pattern evenly, fingers 1-3-2-4-3-5 and back. Press start when you are ready.
Even fingers in time. Same pattern as steady eighth notes at 72 beats per minute. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Golden Train Rag. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Rainy Carousel Song. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Right hand, thumb under C major scale. Pass the thumb under the third finger to play a full octave smoothly.
Here is a magic trick for playing more than five notes. Play C, D, E with fingers one, two, three. Then slide your thumb under your hand to play F. Now keep going up. Listen.
Coming down, your middle finger crosses over your thumb. Get your thumb ready early, so there is no gap in the sound.
C scale up and down. Fingering 1-2-3-1-2-3-4-5, then 5-4-3-2-1-3-2-1. Press start when you are ready.
Scale in time, legato. Connected quarter notes at 66 beats per minute. Hold each key until the next sounds. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Sunny Fox Dance. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Misty Parade Blues. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Right hand, staccato and broken chords. Short bouncy notes, then chord notes played one after another.
A little dot over a note means play it short and bouncy, like touching something hot. Let the key spring right back up. This is called staccato.
C, E, G played one after another is a broken chord. Keep your hand shaped over all three keys, so each finger is ready.
Staccato C-E-G. Short notes eighth note and rest in time at 72 beats per minute. Press start when you are ready.
Broken chords C, F, G, C. Keep the chord shape while playing the notes one at a time. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Midnight Garden Lullaby. The band plays; you play your notes on the strong beats. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Rainy Garden Dance. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Left hand, five-finger patterns. Strengthen the left hand with step and skip patterns in C position.
The left hand is like a mirror of the right. The little finger plays the lowest note. Your fourth and fifth fingers are a bit weaker, so keep them nice and round.
Skips 5-3, 4-2, 3-1. Play C E D F E G and back with 5-3-4-2-3-1. Press start when you are ready.
Left hand in time. Eighth notes at 66 beats per minute, every note equally loud. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Copper Parade Dance. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Midnight Parade Blues. The band plays; you play your notes on the strong beats. Press start when you are ready.
Left hand, cross over C major scale. Cross the third finger over the thumb to play a full octave in the left hand.
For the left hand going up, play C, D, E, F, G with fingers five to one. Then cross your middle finger over your thumb to A, and finish B and C.
Left-hand C scale. Fingering 5-4-3-2-1-3-2-1 up, 1-2-3-1-2-3-4-5 down. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Velvet Teapot Blues. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Sleepy Lighthouse Rag. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Left hand, accompaniment patterns. Alberti bass and the waltz oom-pah-pah, the left-hand patterns behind countless songs.
This left-hand pattern goes low, high, middle, high, C, G, E, G. It is called Alberti bass. Mozart used it a lot. Keep the thumb light. Listen.
This is a waltz pattern. Play one low note, then two soft chords, oom, pah, pah. Lean a little on the oom.
Alberti bass C, G, C. Eighth notes at 63 beats per minute, fingers 5-1-3-1. Press start when you are ready.
Waltz bass oom-pah-pah. Low note, then two light chords, in 3 4 at 80 beats per minute. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Sunny Train March. The band plays; you play your notes on the strong beats. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Wandering Lantern Song. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
The grand staff. Read treble and bass together and pass a melody between the hands.
Piano music uses two staffs joined together. The top one is mostly for the right hand, the bottom one for the left hand. Middle C sits right between them.
Here is an easy rule. Notes on the top staff are for your right hand. Notes on the bottom staff are for your left hand. Check which staff first.
Middle C from both sides. Alternate right hand C finger 1 and left hand C finger 1 reading the grand staff. Press start when you are ready.
Treble or bass?. Notes jump between the staves, play each with the hand of its staff. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Paper Owl Rag. The band plays; you play your notes on the strong beats. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Golden Teapot March. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Melody over a held bass. Right hand moves while the left hand holds long notes.
Now one hand holds while the other moves. Press one long note with your left hand and keep it down. Then let your right hand play the tune.
A whole note lasts four beats. Count one, two, three, four while your right hand plays, and let go when the next low note comes.
C position with a bass C. right hand C D E F G over a held left hand C. Press start when you are ready.
Ode to Joy with bass. First phrase of Ode to Joy over whole-note C and G. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Lucky Teapot Lullaby. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Little Teapot March. The band plays; you play your notes on the strong beats. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Sleepy Harbor March. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Parallel and contrary motion. Both hands play together, moving the same way and in opposite directions.
Both hands moving the same way is called parallel motion. Your right hand starts with the thumb, your left hand with the little finger. Up they go, together.
Now the hands move away from each other, like opening a book. Both thumbs start on middle C. This is called contrary motion. It feels natural, because the finger numbers match.
Parallel five-finger. C D E F G in both hands together, an octave apart. Press start when you are ready.
Contrary from middle C. right hand goes up, left hand goes down, both start with the thumb. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Silver Meadow Rag. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Jolly Parade Blues. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Hands together, chords under a tune. Left hand plays C, F and G chords while the right hand plays a melody.
Your left hand can play small chords too, C, F and G. These shapes only move a tiny bit, so soon you will not even need to look.
Change the chord on beat one, exactly with the tune. Practice the left hand alone first, then add the right hand slowly.
Chord changes. left hand C, F, G, C chords, one bar each. Press start when you are ready.
Melody with chords. right hand melody over the left hand chords. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Rainy Harbor Dance. The band plays the tune; you play the chords. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Rainy Kite Rag. The band plays the tune; you play the chords. Press start when you are ready.
Eighth notes. Two notes per beat, count 1 and 2 and.
An eighth note lasts half a beat, so two of them fit into one beat. They are joined by a little bar on top. Count, one and two and three and four and.
The beat stays the same speed. Eighth notes just fit two notes into each beat. Most people rush them, so count out loud and follow the clicks.
Quarters and eighths. Mix quarters and eighths on C D E. Press start when you are ready.
Running eighths. C position up and down in eighths. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Golden Harbor Song. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Quiet Garden Lullaby. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Dotted rhythms. A dot adds half the value, dotted half, dotted quarter.
A dot after a note makes it longer, by half again. A dotted half note lasts three beats. A dotted quarter is often followed by a short note, long, short.
A dotted rhythm sounds like taaa-ti. You can hear it in Ode to Joy. Feel the long note, then the quick one.
Dotted quarter and eighth. Long-short patterns on C D E. Press start when you are ready.
Dotted half. Three-beat notes in 3 4. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Velvet Meadow Blues. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Silver Lighthouse Rag. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Rests and silence. Silence is counted exactly like sound.
A rest means silence. Every note has a matching rest. During a rest, lift your hand, but keep counting in your head.
The most common mistake is coming in too early after a rest. Say the silent beats out loud, quietly, one, two, three, four.
Play and wait. Notes and quarter rests. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Sunny Parade Blues. The band plays each phrase; you answer with your notes at the end of the bar. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Lucky Comet March. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Three-four time, the waltz. Three beats in a bar, strong first beat.
Some music counts in threes, ONE, two, three, ONE, two, three. The first beat is the strongest. Waltzes and many lullabies go like this.
Left hand plays a low note on beat one, and light chords on beats two and three. Oom, pah, pah. The right hand plays the tune on top.
Waltz bass. left hand oom-pah-pah on C and G. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Quiet Bridge Waltz. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Paper Fox Lullaby. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Ties and syncopation. Notes that start off the beat and hold across it.
A curved line joining two of the same note is a tie. Play the first one and just keep holding, through the second one.
Sometimes a note comes in between the beats and is held over the next beat. That is called syncopation. It makes music bounce and groove.
On the and. Notes start on the off-beat. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Jolly Garden Tune. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Lucky Kite Tune. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Sixteenth notes. Four notes in a beat, and the gallop rhythms they make.
Sixteenth notes have two beams. Four of them fit in one beat. Say ti-ka-ti-ka, nice and even, like rain on a roof.
Mix one eighth note and two sixteenths and you get a gallop, like a horse. Ti-tika is long, short, short. Tika-ti is short, short, long. Say it first, then play it.
Hear the sixteenths. Pick the syllables for the rhythm you hear. Listen, then answer.
Ti-ka-ti-ka. Quarter, then four even sixteenths on each step. Press start when you are ready.
The gallop. Ti-tika and tika-ti, long short short, short short long. Press start when you are ready.
Triplets. Three notes in the time of two, the lilt of blues, gospel and ballads.
A little three over three notes makes a triplet. That means three notes in one beat. Say tri-po-let on every beat, smooth and round.
Now switch between ti-ti and tri-po-let. Keep the beat steady in your head. Only change how you split it. The beat never moves.
Two or three?. Hear each beat split in two or in three, and pick the words. Listen, then answer.
Triplet arpeggios. C E G as triplets, a quarter note on each landing. Press start when you are ready.
Ti-ti, tri-po-let. Eighths then triplets, steady beat. Press start when you are ready.
Two-four, six-eight and cut time. Marches, lilting six-eight, and counting in two.
Two-four has two beats in a bar. Strong, weak. Strong, weak. Like a march. Count one, two, one, two.
Six-eight has six little beats, but it feels like two big ones. Say one-and-a, two-and-a. At first, count all six slowly and lean on one and four.
A C with a line through it is cut time. Count in two big beats, not four. It looks like four-four, but it feels broader and smoother.
Which time is it?. Hear the strong beats and name the time signature. Listen, then answer.
A march in two-four. STRONG weak, crisp and even. Press start when you are ready.
Row along in six-eight. Feel two big beats, long-short, long-short. Press start when you are ready.
Cut time. Four quarters to a bar, felt in two. Press start when you are ready.
The road map, repeats, endings, D.C. and D.S.. Follow the signs that send you back and forward through a piece.
Two dots next to a thick double line mean go back. Play to the end sign, then go back to the start sign, and play that part again.
A bracket with a one is the first ending. Play it the first time. When you come back, skip it and play the bracket with a two.
D.C. means go back to the very beginning. D.S. means go back to the curly S sign. Al Fine means stop at the word Fine. Al Coda means jump to the Coda at the end.
A dot under an arch is a fermata. It looks like a bird's eye. Hold that note a bit longer, then keep going. When you play with others, everyone holds together.
Follow the map. Read the signs and choose the order the bars are played in. Listen, then answer.
D.C. and D.S.. Longer maps with D.C. al Fine, D.S. al Coda and repeats. Listen, then answer.
G major, meet F sharp. The G major scale and its one sharp.
G major has one special note, F sharp. The sharp sign at the start of each line means every F becomes F sharp, the black key just to its right.
The fingering is the same as C major. Your fourth finger plays the F sharp in the right hand.
G major scale right hand. One octave up and down. Press start when you are ready.
G major scale left hand. One octave, left hand. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Morning Owl Tune. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Silver Market Lullaby. The band plays; you play your notes on the strong beats. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Golden Lighthouse Lullaby. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
F major, meet B flat. The F major scale, one flat and a special fingering.
A flat means one key lower, to the left. F major has one flat, B flat. That is the black key between A and B.
In F major the thumb crosses after the fourth finger, so your thumb never has to land on the black key.
F major scale right hand. One octave with 1 2 3 4 1 2 3 4. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Midnight Bridge Tune. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Silver River March. The band plays; you play your notes on the strong beats. Press start when you are ready.
Key signatures and the natural sign. Read the sharps or flats at the start of the line, and cancel them with a natural.
Instead of writing a sharp next to every F, music puts it once at the start of each line. That's the key signature. It counts for that letter everywhere, all the way through.
Sharps always come in the same order, starting with F. With sharps, go up one key from the last sharp to name the key. One sharp means G major. One flat means F major.
A natural sign cancels a sharp or flat. Play the white key. It lasts until the end of the bar, then the key signature comes back.
Name the key. See the key signature and choose the major key. Listen, then answer.
G major with a natural. Every F is sharp, except where the natural sign says so. Press start when you are ready.
F major with a natural. Every B is flat, until the natural sign. Press start when you are ready.
D major and two sharps. F sharp and C sharp, the key of many violin and gospel songs.
D major has two sharps, F sharp and C sharp. Sharps always come in the same order, so two sharps always means F sharp and C sharp.
D major scale right hand. One octave, 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Golden Bridge Blues. You play every note of the tune that uses your keys; the band fills in the rest. Press start when you are ready.
Play along, Lucky Kite March. Keep time with the band, your notes come exactly on the beat. Press start when you are ready.
A minor. The relative minor of C, natural and harmonic forms.
A minor uses the same white keys as C major, but its home note is A. That makes it sound darker, a little more serious. Listen.
Raise the seventh note, so G becomes G sharp. Now the music pulls strongly back home to A. You hear this in lots of film and folk music.

Octaves and jumps. Hand stretches and leaps with accuracy.
An octave is eight white keys, from one C to the next C. Stretch your thumb and little finger. Keep your wrist loose and drop into the keys.
For a big jump, look at where you are going and get your hand ready before you need it. Being ready beats being fast.

Fingering, crossings, substitution and choosing. How to find a fingering that works, and the two tricks that make long lines smooth.
To go up, your thumb slides under your third or fourth finger. To go down, those fingers cross over your thumb. Keep your wrist level and move your thumb early.
Finger substitution means holding a key down and quietly swapping fingers on it, without letting go. It helps you play smoothly when you run out of fingers.
Before you play, look at the shape of the music. Put your thumb on white keys, plan your crossings, and write your fingering in. Then use it every time.
Crossings up and down. A long line with planned crossings fingers shown. Press start when you are ready.

Pedal like a pianist. Legato after-the-beat pedaling, half pedal, and knowing when to leave it off.
Play the chord, then press the pedal just after. At the next chord, lift the pedal as you play, and press it again right after. Up with your hands, down after your hands.
Half pedal means pressing only part of the way down. It makes the sound less blurry without stopping it.
Don't use the pedal for short, bouncy notes or fast low scales. If it sounds muddy, lift it more often. Let your ears decide.
Chords, pedaled legato. Slow chords, lift and catch the pedal on each change watch and listen. Press start when you are ready.

Minor scales, natural, harmonic and melodic. Three versions of the minor scale and why each exists.
Natural minor in A uses only white keys, from A to A. It has the same notes as C major, but it sounds calm and a bit sad.
Harmonic minor raises the seventh note, G becomes G sharp. That makes the music pull strongly back home.
Melodic minor raises two notes going up, F sharp and G sharp, for a smooth climb. Coming down, it goes back to natural minor.
Three A minors. Natural, harmonic, then melodic up and down. Press start when you are ready.
Ornaments, grace notes, mordents, trills and tremolo. The little decorations that make a melody speak.
A grace note is a tiny note squeezed in just before the main note. Play them almost together, and let the main note ring.
A mordent is a quick wiggle, the note, the note above, and back again. A turn goes above, main, below, main.
A trill goes back and forth quickly between two neighbour notes. A tremolo goes back and forth between notes further apart. Stay loose. Speed comes from relaxing.
Written-out ornaments. A mordent, a turn and a short trill, slowly then in time. Press start when you are ready.
Octave tremolo. Left hand alternates C and C, loose and even. Press start when you are ready.
Right hand in thirds, soprano and alto. Play two notes at once in the right hand, the way a pianist plays the soprano and alto parts.
In choir songs, the right hand often plays two singers at once, the tune on top, and a helper part just below it. Most often they are a third apart. That means you skip one white key. Listen.
For thirds, use fingers one and three, then two and four, then three and five, as you climb. Keep your hand still, and press both keys at exactly the same moment.
The tune is on top. Lean a tiny bit more on your top finger, so the tune sings a little louder than the helper part. Listen to the difference.
If you hear two clicks instead of one sound, the notes are not together yet. Go slowly. Play each pair, stop, check, then move on.
Thirds up and down. C and E to G and B and back, fingers 1-3, 2-4, 3-5. Press start when you are ready.
Thirds through the scale. Thirds from C up to C and back. Press start when you are ready.
Ode to Joy with an alto. The melody on top, the alto a third below. Press start when you are ready.
Right hand in sixths and mixed intervals. Wider pairs, and moving between 3rds, 4ths and 6ths as real harmony parts do.
A sixth is a wider pair, like C up to A. Use your thumb and little finger. Sixths sound warm and open. Listen.
A real helper part does not stay the same distance below the tune. It moves to the nearest good note, so the gap keeps changing. Watch both notes in every pair.
In sixths your thumb plays the lower note. Keep it light, and keep your top fingers round, so the tune stays smooth.
Sixths up and down. C and A to G and E and back, fingers 1 and 5. Press start when you are ready.
3rds to 6ths. Alternate a third and a sixth on each step. Press start when you are ready.
A two-part hymn line. Soprano and alto from a hymn, the gap changes as the harmony moves. Press start when you are ready.
Left hand in two notes, fifths, sixths and the shuffle. Two notes at once in the left hand, power fifths, sixths, and the rock and roll shuffle.
Now the left hand plays two notes, the bottom note and the note five keys up. Use your little finger and your thumb. This sound is the backbone of rock and folk music. Listen.
Keep your little finger on C, and rock your top finger between G and A, G, A, G, A. This is the shuffle, the left hand of lots of blues and rock and roll songs. Listen.
In choir music, the left hand plays two singers at once, the tenor and the bass. Read both notes on the bottom staff and press them together.
left hand fifths. C, F, G, C, root and fifth together. Press start when you are ready.
The shuffle. Fifth to sixth and back on C, F and G. Press start when you are ready.
Tenor and bass. Two parts in the left hand, read from the bass staff. Press start when you are ready.

Read from the bottom up. Find the lowest note first, it tells you the chord. Then the top note, that is the tune. Then fill in the middle.
If a note stays the same in the next chord, keep that finger down and only move the others. It sounds smooth, just like a choir.

How playing by ear works. The method musicians use to work out any song, home note, bass, chords, melody.
Here is a secret. Good ears do not hear letter names. They hear how notes relate to a home note, like a family. Learn these patterns once, and you can play a song in any key. Listen.
To work out any song, go step by step. First, find the home note. Second, hum the low notes, the bass. Third, work out the chords. Fourth, find the tune. Fifth, put it all together.
Never try a whole song at once. Take one short line, play it again and again, and sing it back first. If you can sing it, you can find it on the piano.
Your ears grow like muscles. A few minutes every day works much better than a long time once a week. These drills will train each step.
Where is home?. Hear a short tune in a random key and play its home note. Listen, then answer.
Do, mi, sol. Hear the key, then one note, is it 1, 3 or 5? Listen, then answer.
Find the key of any song. Find the home note, decide major or minor, and work out which notes the song uses.
Home is the note where the song rests, usually the very last note. Hum it. Then try notes on the piano until one sounds like it belongs, completely settled. Listen.
Once you have home, sing up from it, do, re, mi. If mi sounds bright and happy, the song is major. If it sounds darker, the song is minor. Listen to both.
Each key uses seven notes. C major uses only the white keys. When you know the key, you only have seven notes to search, instead of twelve.
You can always work a song out in an easy key, like C, and move it later to fit a singer. The pattern stays the same.
Find home in any key. Hear a tune and play its home note. Keys change every round. Listen, then answer.
Major or minor chord. Bright or dark? Train the difference that decides the key. Listen, then answer.
Major or minor third. Hear the key, then the third. Is it mi major or me minor? Listen, then answer.
The sound of each scale degree. Functional ear training, every note in a key has its own pull. Learn to feel it.
Every note in a key has its own feeling. Do, mi and sol feel calm and settled. The other notes lean towards them, like they want to go somewhere. Listen to each one.
Not sure which note it is? Sing from it back home to do, by the shortest path. Ti steps up to do. Fa walks down, fa, mi, re, do. Listen.
A single note means nothing on its own. Always hear the key first, with a few chords. Then the note will tell you who it is. Listen.
Songs you know can help. Do, re, mi is one, two, three. Twinkle Twinkle starts one, one, five, five. Amazing Grace starts five, one.
Degrees 1 to 5. Hear the key, then a note from do to sol. Listen, then answer.
All seven degrees. The full major scale. Listen for the pull. Listen, then answer.
Degrees in any key. Same skill, keys all over the keyboard. Listen, then answer.
Melodies, contour and intervals. Follow a tune note to note, direction, step or leap, and how far.
Before you look for notes, draw the shape of the tune in the air with your hand, up, down, or the same. Most tunes move in small steps, with a jump now and then. Listen.
Each jump has a sound you can link to a song. Twinkle Twinkle jumps a fifth. Here Comes the Bride jumps a fourth. When you hear a jump, test it against your songs. Listen.
Find one note you are sure about, often the first one or the home note. Then work out from there, one note at a time.
Let's try Amazing Grace. It starts on sol and jumps up to do. Listen, then work out the first line by ear in the exercises.
Steps and small leaps. Name the interval, 2nds, 3rds and the fifth. Listen, then answer.
Big leaps. 4ths, 5ths, 6ths and the octave, up and down. Listen, then answer.

When the Saints, line 1. Hear the key, then the tune. It starts on C. Press listen first.
Hear the bass, find the chords. The bass line tells you the chords. Hum it, find it, then decide major or minor.
The low notes tell you the chords. In most songs, the bass plays the name of each chord. Hum the lowest sound you hear and find it on the piano. Listen.
Each key has its own family of chords. In C major, C, F and G are happy major chords. D, E and A are minor chords. So once you find the bass, you often know the chord already. Listen.
Bass notes often step to a neighbor, or jump to a strong partner. When the bass drops from G to C, that almost always means the song is going home. Listen.
Sometimes the bass plays a different note of the chord, to make a smooth walking line. If a chord sounds right but the bass sounds odd, try a chord that contains that bass note.
Bass of I, four, five. Hear the home chord, then four chords. Play each bass note. Listen, then answer.
Bass with the six chord. Now with the minor six chord in the mix. Listen, then answer.
Progressions you hear everywhere. Recognize the handful of chord patterns behind most songs.
A few groups of four chords are used in thousands of songs. Learn how they sound, and you will start to recognize songs on the first listen. Listen.
Each chord has a feeling. One is rest. Four is a lift away. Five is a question that wants an answer. Six is the sad cousin of one. Listen to them.
Musicians often call chords by numbers instead of names. One, five, six, four works in every key. It is like a secret code that travels anywhere.
Name the chords. Four chords after the home chord. Name each one, I, four, five or six. Listen, then answer.
Add the two chord. Now two joins in the chord before five. Listen, then answer.
Major, minor, diminished. The three chord types inside a key. Listen, then answer.
Work out a whole song. Put the method together on Amazing Grace, key, bass, chords, melody, both hands.
Let's work out a whole song, Amazing Grace. Step one, the key. It ends on C, with a happy C chord. So home is C, and it is major. It sways in threes.
Step two, the bass. Hum the low notes. They sit on C, move to F, back to C, then to G. Listen.
Step three, the chords. Bass C means a C chord. F means an F chord. G means a G chord. Listen.
Step four, the tune. It starts on G, jumps up to C, climbs to E, comes down through D to C, dips to A, and lands on G. Listen.
Step five, play it! Right hand plays the tune. Left hand plays the low note at the start of each bar. You worked out a whole song by ear. Well done!
Find the bass by ear. Hear the key, then the bass line of the first two lines. Play it back. Press listen first.
Find line 2 by ear. The second line ends higher, on D. Starts on G. Press listen first.
Both hands. Melody plus the roots you found. Press start when you are ready.
Any song, any key. Because you think in numbers, you can play what you hear in any key.

Play along with your favorite songs every day, even just the low notes. Start with songs that have only a few chords. Soon you will hear the patterns right away.

Saints in G. Same tune in G. Starts on G. Press listen first.
Chords in any key. Name the progression wherever it is played. Listen, then answer.
Jazz harmony, seventh chords. Jazz is built on four-note chords. Learn the five types and the seventh chords of a key.
Jazz loves richer chords. Add one more note on top of a normal chord and you get a seventh chord. It sounds fuller, and it wants to keep moving. Listen.
Here are five kinds of seventh chords on the same note. Each one has its own color, some dreamy, some bluesy, some spooky. Listen to them one by one.
If you build seventh chords on every note of C major, you get seven chords. Only one of them, G seven, has that strong pull back home. Listen.
Jazz music writes chords as short codes, like C major seven, or G seven. Once you know the codes, you can read any jazz song.
Five seventh chords on C. Play each type. Feel how one note changes the color. Press start when you are ready.
seventh chords of C major. Climb the key in seventh chords, right hand. Press start when you are ready.

Swing feel and jazz rhythm. Long-short eighths, accents off the beat, and the Charleston rhythm for comping.
Jazz eighth notes are not even. Play them long, short, long, short. Say doo-ba, doo-ba. That bouncy feeling is called swing. Listen.
In swing, the strong beats are two and four. Snap your fingers on two and four, and make the in-between notes pop a little. That makes the music bounce.
Jazz pianists play short chord stabs instead of long chords. This is called comping. A favorite rhythm hits beat one, and just before beat two. It is called the Charleston. Listen.
Jazz players often play the next chord a little early, just before the beat. This push makes the music lean forward and feel exciting.
Swing eighths. Play the line long-short. The scoring expects swung timing. Press start when you are ready.
Charleston comping. C six shell on beat 1 and the and of 2, every bar. Press start when you are ready.
Off-beat phrase. A swing phrase that starts and ends off the beat. Press start when you are ready.
The two, five, one and guide tones. The most important progression in jazz, played with shells and smooth guide-tone lines.
The two, five, one is jazz's favorite little sentence. Two gets ready. Five builds tension. One brings it home. Listen.
Jazz pianists often play just two notes in the left hand, the bottom note and one color note. This is called a shell. It is simple, and it sounds great. Listen.
Watch the color notes from chord to chord. They only move a tiny bit, or stay the same. If you play just these, people can still hear the chords. Listen and compare.
Learn the two, five, one in a few keys, starting with C, F and B flat. The shapes stay the same. Only the starting note moves.
Shells in C. left hand shells, D minor seven, G seven, C major seven. Press start when you are ready.

two, five, one in F and B flat. Shells in two more keys. Press start when you are ready.

Rootless voicings. The modern jazz piano sound, third, seventh and colors ninth, 13th in the left hand, no root.
In a band, the bass player plays the bottom notes. So the piano can leave them out and play just the colorful notes. Jazz players call this rootless. Listen.
Here is one shape for rootless chords. Each note only moves a little, or stays still, from chord to chord. Listen to how smooth it is.
Here is a second shape, with the notes stacked a different way. Use whichever one sits nicer on the piano. Listen.
Keep these left-hand chords around the middle of the piano. If they go too low, they sound muddy.

B-form two, five, one. The other shape. Press start when you are ready.
Comp in swing. A-form voicings, Charleston rhythm. Press start when you are ready.
The blues, form, scale and phrasing. The 12-bar jazz blues, the blues scale, crushed notes and call and response.
The blues is twelve bars long, and it repeats. It uses bluesy seventh chords all the way through. Count the bars as you listen. Listen.
The blues scale has six notes that make anything sound bluesy. One note in the middle is extra special. Slide through it, do not stop on it. Listen.
A piano can't bend notes like a guitar, so we crush them. Play two neighbor keys almost together, sliding off the first one. It sounds like a singer's bluesy slide. Listen.
Blues phrases talk to each other. Play a short idea, like a question. Leave a little space. Then answer it. Space is just as important as notes.
F blues shells. left hand root and seventh or third through the whole form. Press start when you are ready.
Blues scale and crush. Up the F blues scale, then a crushed-note phrase. Press start when you are ready.
Call and response. A two-bar call, the same answer moved to the B flat seven chord. Press start when you are ready.
Improvising, chord tones and approach notes. Make lines that outline the chords, target chord tones, approach them, enclose them.
To make up a jazz tune that fits, land on a chord note on the strong beats. Those notes always sound right. Listen.
Here is a jazz trick. Play the key right below your target note, just before it. That tiny bit of tension makes the target sound great. Listen.
Another trick, surround your target. Play the note above it, then the note below it, then land on it. Listen.
Start with a tiny idea of three to five notes. Repeat it, then change it a little. Good solos tell a story from one small idea.

Enclosures. Above, below, target, into F, B and E. Press start when you are ready.
Walking bass and two-hand comping. Walk a bass line in the left hand while the right hand comps.
A walking bass plays one note on every beat. Beat one is the chord's name note. Beats two and three are chord notes or neighbors. Beat four leads into the next chord. Listen.
Sneaking in from the key right next door makes the next chord sound like it had to happen. That is the walking bass player's secret.
While the left hand walks, the right hand plays short, light chords. Keep them gentle, so the bass line can breathe.
Walk a two, five, one. left hand quarter notes, root on beat 1, approach on beat 4. Press start when you are ready.
Walk and comp. left hand walks, right hand comps guide tones on beat 2. Press start when you are ready.
Reharmonization, turnarounds and substitutes. Secondary dominants, the tritone substitute, and the turnarounds that link phrases.
You can make any chord sound more exciting by playing its own five chord just before it. It is like a little arrow pointing at the next chord. Listen and compare.
Two different chords, G seven and D flat seven, share the same important notes. So jazz players swap one for the other. The bass then slides down smoothly. Listen and compare.
A turnaround is a short group of chords at the end of a section that leads you back to the start. Listen.
Turnaround one, six seven, two, five. Shells through the classic turnaround. Press start when you are ready.
Tritone substitute. D minor seven, D flat seven, C major seven, the bass slides down. Press start when you are ready.
Hear the turnarounds. Which version is it? Listen, then answer.
Play from a lead sheet. Melody in the right hand, shells in the left, swing feel, a real jazz performance.
A lead sheet only shows the tune and the chord names. You decide how to play the rest. This is how jazz musicians read songs.
Start simple. Right hand plays the tune, with swing. Left hand plays a simple shell on each chord. Add more when that feels easy.
Let's play When the Saints, jazz style. The tune starts F, A, B flat, C. Listen.
Saints, melody and shells. right hand melody, left hand shells on beat 1. Swing it. Press start when you are ready.
Four voices, ranges and spacing. Soprano, alto, tenor, bass, where each one sings, how far apart, and which note to double.
Choirs sing in four parts, soprano, alto, tenor and bass. Each part is its own little tune. Together they make the harmony. Listen.
Each voice has notes it can sing comfortably. Sopranos sing high, basses sing low. Keep each part in its comfortable zone, so nobody strains. Listen.
Keep the top three voices close together, no more than an octave apart. The bass can be further away. And voices should not cross over each other. Listen and compare.
A chord has three notes, but a choir has four voices, so one note is sung twice. Usually we double the bottom note of the chord. Never leave out the middle note. Listen and compare.
Play I, four, five in four parts. left hand bass and tenor, right hand alto and soprano. Press start when you are ready.
Complete the chord, find the alto. The alto is hidden. Which chord note is missing? Play all four. Press start when you are ready.
Complete the chord, find the tenor. The tenor is hidden. Remember, double the root, keep the third. Press start when you are ready.
Voice leading, the rules. Common tones, step-wise motion, contrary motion, and no parallel 5ths or octaves.
If two chords share a note, let the same voice keep singing it. It sounds smooth, and it is easy to sing. Listen.
Each voice moves to the closest note of the next chord. Small steps are easy to sing. Leave the big jumps to the bass. Listen and compare.
When the bass goes up, let the other voices go down, and the other way round. It keeps every part independent and interesting. Listen.
Two voices should not move together in fifths or octaves. It makes two singers sound like one, and the music sounds empty. Listen to the wrong way, then the right way.
Some notes really want to move. The note just below home wants to step up to home. Follow these pulls and your endings will sound strong. Listen.
Smooth one, six, two, five, one. Watch common tones held and voices moving by step. Press start when you are ready.
Find the alto by voice leading. Hidden alto, keep common tones, move by step. Press start when you are ready.
Resolve the tendency tones. five seven to I, the seventh falls, the leading tone rises. Alto and soprano hidden. Press start when you are ready.
Cadences, how phrases end. Perfect, plagal, half and deceptive cadences, punctuation for music.
The perfect cadence is a full stop. The five chord goes to the one chord, and the music sounds finished. Listen.
The plagal cadence sounds like the Amen at the end of a hymn. Four goes to one. It is soft and peaceful. Listen.
A half cadence is like a comma. The music stops on the five chord, and you feel there is more to come. Listen.
A deceptive cadence is a surprise. You expect home, but you land on the sad six chord instead. Listen to the difference.
A song often asks a question, then answers it. The first line ends with a comma, and the second line ends with a full stop. Plan these endings first.
The four cadences. Perfect, plagal, half, deceptive. Press start when you are ready.
Find the bass of each cadence. Bass hidden, which root makes each cadence? Press start when you are ready.
Hear the ending. Which chords end the phrase? Listen, then answer.
Inversions and a singable bass line. Put the third or fifth in the bass to make the bass line move smoothly.
Put a different chord note in the bass, and the chord sounds lighter. It also lets the bass walk smoothly instead of jumping. Listen and compare.
Using these, the bass can walk down step by step, like going down stairs. This sound is in lots of songs and wedding music. Listen.
Some bass notes sound unsteady, so we only use them in special places, like just before the final ending. Listen.
The descending bass line. C, G over B, A minor, A minor or G, F, C over E, D minor, G, C. Press start when you are ready.
Write the bass, find it. Upper voices given, bass hidden. Make the line step down. Press start when you are ready.
Cadential 6 4. four, one six or 4, five, one, the classic strong ending. Press start when you are ready.
Harmonize a melody, step by step. From a bare tune to four parts, cadences, chord choice, bass line, inner voices.
To add harmony to a tune, start with the endings. If a line ends on the home note, end it with a full stop. If not, end it with a comma.
Every tune note fits in a few different chords. Pick a chord for the important notes, the ones on the strong beats. Listen to the choices.
Chords like to travel in a circle, home, then away, then tension, then back home. Change chords once or twice a bar, and keep it steady.
Make the bass a second tune. When the top goes up, let the bass go down. Step where you can, and use the chord's name note at the endings.
Now fill in the middle voices with the closest notes. Then sing or play each part alone. Each one should be easy to sing.
In Voice, you can sing a tune into Sing to score and choose four parts. Auxa follows these same rules. Compare its ideas with yours.
Twinkle, choose the bass. The tune in half notes, inner voices given. Find the bass for one, one, four, one, four, one, five, one. Press start when you are ready.
Twinkle, fill the inner voices. Soprano and bass given. Find alto and tenor. Press start when you are ready.
Non-chord tones, passing, neighbor, suspension. Notes outside the chord that add motion and expression.
A passing note fills the gap between two chord notes, step by step. It makes the line flow, without changing the chord. Listen and compare.
A neighbor note steps away and comes right back, like a little decoration.
A suspension holds a note from the last chord for a moment, then lets it fall to where it belongs. It sounds tender and beautiful. Listen and compare.
Passing tone in the alto. The alto steps E, D, C while the chord holds. Press start when you are ready.
A 4, 3 suspension cadence. Hold C over the G bass, then fall to B, then resolve home. Press start when you are ready.
Piano accompaniment styles. One progression, many textures, block, broken, Alberti, ballad, stride.
An arrangement keeps the same chords, but changes how they are played. Blocks sound like a hymn. Broken chords sound like a ballad. Listen.
For slow songs, play a low note, then spread the chord upwards, one note at a time. Use the pedal to let it ring. Listen.
Stride piano jumps, a low note on beats one and three, a chord in the middle on beats two and four. It is the sound of old ragtime piano. Listen.
For pop songs, the left hand plays simple low notes, and the right hand plays chords in a bouncy rhythm. Leave space for the singer.
Broken chords. C, A minor, F, G, broken in eighths. Press start when you are ready.
Stride. Bass on 1 and 3, chord on 2 and 4. Press start when you are ready.
Ballad arpeggios with melody. right hand melody, left hand arpeggio under it. Press start when you are ready.
Arrange a song for choir. From a tune to a full soprano, alto, tenor and bass arrangement, key, texture, harmony parts, intro and ending.
To arrange a song for a choir, you need the tune and the chords. You can work them out by ear, or sing the tune into Sing to score.
Put the tune where the sopranos can sing it comfortably. If it is too low, give the tune to the tenors instead, and add harmony around it.
Do not use all four parts the whole time. Start with everyone singing the tune together, add a harmony part, then save the full four parts for the chorus.
The sopranos sing the tune. The bass makes a good low line. The alto and tenor fill in with the closest notes. Then sing each part alone to check it.
Here is Amazing Grace in four parts. Listen to it together, then learn each part on its own. That is how choirs rehearse.
Amazing Grace, soprano, alto, tenor and bass. Play the four-part setting, line 1. Press start when you are ready.
Learn the alto part. Alto line alone, as a choir alto would rehearse it. Press start when you are ready.
Learn the tenor part. Tenor line alone written an octave lower than it sounds. Press start when you are ready.
Hymns in two parts, tune and bass. Read a hymn score and play its two outside voices, the melody and the bass line.

A hymn has four singers written on two lines of music. On top, soprano sings the tune, and alto sings under it. On the bottom, tenor, and bass, the lowest. Your right hand plays the top two. Your left hand plays the bottom two.
Start with the outside parts, the tune on top and the bass at the bottom. Those two together already sound full enough for people to sing with. Learn each hand alone first, then put them together.
This tune is called Old Hundredth. It is more than four hundred and fifty years old, and churches all over the world sing it. Every note is one beat. At the end of each line, everyone takes a breath.
Lines 1 and 2, tune and bass. Soprano in the right hand, bass in the left, Old Hundredth. Press start when you are ready.
Whole hymn, tune and bass. All four lines, tune and bass. Press start when you are ready.
Three parts, alto joins the right hand. Soprano and alto together in the right hand over the bass.
Now the alto joins your right hand, just under the tune. Play the tune with your outside fingers, four and five, so it sings out. Your thumb side plays the alto, a little softer.
When the tune moves but the alto stays, keep the alto key held down. Don't let it go early, or the hymn sounds thin.
Amazing Grace has three beats in a bar, like a gentle waltz. It starts on beat three. Count three, then one two three, one two three, and lean softly on each one.
Old Hundredth in three parts. Lines 1 and 2, soprano and alto in the right hand, bass in the left. Press start when you are ready.
Amazing Grace in three parts. The first half of the hymn, tune, alto and bass. Press start when you are ready.
Four parts, the full hymn. Tenor joins the left hand and you play the hymn as written.
Now the tenor joins your left hand. It is the top note on the bottom staff. Read the bass first, then add the tenor just above it.
Read each beat as one chord shape, from the bottom up, bass, tenor, alto, soprano. Your eyes see the shape, and your hands move there in one go. Go slowly, one hand at a time, then together.
If a hand can't reach all its notes, give one note to the other hand. Your left thumb can help the alto, or your right thumb can help the tenor. What matters is the sound, not which hand plays it.
Old Hundredth, lines 1 and 2. All four voices. Press start when you are ready.
Old Hundredth, the whole hymn. All four voices, all four lines. Press start when you are ready.
Joyful, joyful in four parts. The Hymn to Joy, first half, all four voices. Press start when you are ready.
Make a hard hymn playable. Three honest ways to simplify, so you can play for singing this Sunday.
When a hymn is too hard, keep what the singers need most, the tune, a steady beat, and the right chords. The middle notes are extra. Make it simpler until you can play it well.
The first easy way, play just the tune and the bass. It is clear, simple, and always right.
The second easy way, your right hand plays the tune. Your left hand holds two notes of the chord, the root and the fifth, for the whole bar.
The third way, your right hand plays full chords on every beat, and your left hand plays the bass in big octaves. This sounds strong for a big room full of people.
Amazing Grace, tune over roots. Tune in the right hand, root and fifth held in the left. Press start when you are ready.
Joyful, joyful, tune and bass. The whole tune with its bass line only. Press start when you are ready.
Introductions, tempo, fermatas and Amen. Give the congregation the tune, the speed and the starting note, and end with an Amen.
Before people sing, play the last line of the hymn as an introduction. It tells them the tune, the starting note, and how fast to go. Then breathe together and begin.
Pick a speed where one breath lasts a whole line. Too slow, and people run out of air. Too fast, and the words get jumbled. Sing the words quietly to yourself while you play.
A fermata at the end of a line means hold and breathe. Hold the chord a little longer, lift your hands, and come back in together on the next line.
Many hymns end with Amen, sung on two chords, chord four, then chord one. It's called the church cadence. Play it slowly and warmly.
Amen in four keys. four to I in C, G, F and D. Press start when you are ready.
Play the introduction. The last line of Old Hundredth in four parts, in time, at singing speed. Press start when you are ready.
Leading the singing. Keep a steady beat for a room full of people, breathe with them, and shape the verses.
Everyone follows the piano, so keep your beat steady, even if the singing slows down. Play the tune and the bass a little louder than the middle notes.
At the end of each line, lift the last chord a tiny bit early so everyone can breathe. Then come back in right on the beat. The beat never stops.
Play softer when the words are gentle, and fuller when they are joyful. On the last verse, add a low bass note for a big finish. Between verses, keep the beat going.
Tune and bass, in time. Old Hundredth, tune and bass, steady at singing speed. Press start when you are ready.
Amazing Grace, in time. Tune, alto and bass in three-four, a steady lilt. Press start when you are ready.
Play from chord symbols. Read letters like G, C, D seven and E minor above a tune and turn them into chords at once.

Chord symbols are letters above the music. A letter on its own, like G, means a major chord. A small m, like E m, means minor. A seven adds one more note. A slash tells you which note goes in the bass.
Every key has a family of chords. Chords one, four, and five are major. Chords two, three, and six are minor. In the key of G, the family is G, A minor, B minor, C, D, and E minor.
Don't jump around for every chord. Keep your right hand near middle C and move each finger to the closest note of the next chord. Your left hand plays the root, the chord's main note.
C F G C. Close right-hand chords over left-hand roots, two beats each. Press start when you are ready.
G E minor C D seven G. The chord family of G, staying close. Press start when you are ready.
A minor D minor G C. Minor chords and a close voice-leading circle. Press start when you are ready.
Electronic keyboard and organ. Use a keyboard's voices, styles and split well, and play legato the way organists do.
On a keyboard, the voice button picks the sound, like piano or organ. The style button adds drums and a band, so keep it soft in church. Split gives your left hand a different sound, like a bass.
Transpose moves everything up or down, so you can play in an easy key. It is handy, but learn the real keys too. When the keyboard is off, what you know stays with you.
Some keyboards play a whole chord when you press one key. It helps at the start, but it can guess wrong. Learn to play the chords yourself as soon as you can.
On an organ, the sound stops the moment you let go. So hold every note for its full length, and join it smoothly to the next one. If two chords share a note, just keep holding it.
On an organ, start with a soft, normal sound, called an eight-foot stop. Add a four-foot stop to make it brighter. Your feet play the bass on the pedals, so your left hand only plays the tenor.
Organ-style hymn line. Old Hundredth lines 1 and 2 in four parts, play every note its full value, perfectly connected. Press start when you are ready.
The pedal line. The bass line alone, as your feet would play it on an organ, steady and connected. Press start when you are ready.
Four chords, a thousand songs. I, five, six and four, the progression under countless pop, worship and Afrobeats songs, with a real groove.
Four chords make thousands of songs, C, G, A minor, and F. Keep your right hand close, moving only a little between chords. Your left hand plays the main note of each chord.
Now add a groove. Play long, long, short, on one, on the and of two, and on four. Count one, two and, three, four. That's the heartbeat of pop music.
For lots of energy, play the low note in octaves on every beat. For a gentle song, just hold the low note for the whole bar.
C G A minor F. Close chords over roots, a bar each. Press start when you are ready.
The pop groove. Long, long, short in the right hand, 1, and-of-2, 4. Press start when you are ready.
Octave drive. Left hand roots in octaves on every beat; the band holds the chords. Press start when you are ready.
Left-hand patterns. Alternating bass, broken chords and open arpeggios, three ways to make a left hand move.
Alternating bass means the main note on beat one, and the fifth on beat three. For C, that's C, then G. It gives a happy bounce.
Broken chords go root, fifth, octave, fifth, in even little notes. One, five, eight, five. It keeps a slow song moving gently.
Open arpeggios go wider, root, fifth, then a high third. One, five, ten, five. It sounds big and rich, and leaves room for your right hand.
Alternating bass. Root and fifth under C, A minor, F and G. Press start when you are ready.
Broken chords, 1 5 8 5. Even eighths under the same chords. Press start when you are ready.
Open arpeggios, 1 5 10 5. A wide, rich left hand. Press start when you are ready.
Colour chords, sus, add2, 6 and augmented. Small changes to a triad that make songs shimmer, ache or lift.
Swap the middle note of a chord for the note above it, and you get a sus four. It sounds like it's waiting. When the middle note comes back, it feels like coming home.
Add one extra note to a chord for new colours. Add the second for a bright, modern sound. Add the sixth for a warm, old-fashioned sound.
Raise the top note of a C chord by one key, and you get augmented. It sounds like a question, and it wants to move on to the next chord.
Colours on C. C sus four to C, Csus2 to C, Cadd2, C six, then C augmented resolving to F. Press start when you are ready.
A worship-style turnaround. Cadd2, G over B, A minor seven, Fsus2 in time. Press start when you are ready.
Twelve-bar blues and boogie-woogie. The twelve-bar form, the boogie left hand, and the blues scale on top.
The blues has twelve bars and three chords. Four bars of C, two of F, two of C, then G, F, C, C. Count the bars out loud at first.
The boogie left hand walks up and down the chord in quick notes. Then you move the same shape to F and to G. Play it with a little swing, long short, long short.
The blues scale is C, E flat, F, F sharp, G, B flat, C. The blue notes rub a little on purpose. That's what makes the blues sound bluesy.
Boogie left hand, twelve bars. The walking eighth-note pattern through the whole form. Press start when you are ready.
The blues scale. Up and down in C. Press start when you are ready.
A riff over the boogie. One riff, four times; the band plays the boogie. Press start when you are ready.
Ragtime and stride. The oom-pah left hand and a syncopated right hand.
Oom-pah! A low note on beats one and three, and a chord in the middle on beats two and four. Your left hand jumps, so look ahead and move early.
Ragtime chords pull each other along, C, A seven, D seven, G seven, and back to C. Each chord leads to the next one.
In ragtime, the right hand plays between the beats while the left hand keeps perfect time. Practise the left hand until it runs all by itself.
Stride left hand. Bass and chord through C, A seven, D seven, G seven, C. Press start when you are ready.
A rag tune. Syncopated right hand; the band plays the stride. Press start when you are ready.
Latin, montuno and bossa nova. The looping salsa piano figure and the gentle Brazilian comp.
A montuno is a short pattern that loops round and round in salsa music. Keep it light, even, and right in time. The groove comes from repeating it.
In Latin music, the bass often comes in a little early, before the chord changes. Listen to the band and feel where it lands.
Bossa nova is soft and gentle. Play close to the keys, quietly, with your right hand just after the beat, like talking softly.
Montuno, C F G F. Right-hand octaves and chord tones; the band plays the bass. Press start when you are ready.
Bossa comp. A minor seven, D seven, G major seven, C major seven, right hand off the beat, left hand root and fifth. Press start when you are ready.
Gospel piano. Walk-ups, passing chords, rich 2-5-1 endings and the church Amen with a twist.
Gospel bass lines walk step by step into the next chord, C, D, E, F. Then they walk back down to come home.
Gospel players add extra notes to their chords to make them rich, like Sunday morning. Play the low notes in octaves to make it strong.
Here's a special Amen. Between F and C, slip in F minor. Just one note moves down a little, A to A flat. Listen to how tender it sounds.
Walk up to four and home. Passing chords over a walking bass. Press start when you are ready.
A Sunday 2-5-1. D minor nine, G thirteen, C major nine with octave bass. Press start when you are ready.
Amen with the minor four. F, F minor, C, listen to the A flat. Press start when you are ready.
Highlife and Afrobeat keys. The bright guitar-like patterns of highlife and the tight, punchy stabs of Afrobeat.
Highlife comes from West Africa, from brass bands and guitar music. On keys, play rippling broken chords, like a guitar, over a bouncy bass. Bright and happy.
Afrobeat is one long groove, often on one minor chord. The keys play short, punchy chords between the beats, and leave gaps. The gaps are part of the rhythm.
Every instrument has its own little pattern, and they fit together like a puzzle. Play yours the same every time and listen to the bass.
Highlife ripple. Broken chords in eighths over C, F, G, C; the band plays the bass. Press start when you are ready.
Afrobeat stabs. Short chords on the off-beats over a minor groove; the band plays the bass riff. Press start when you are ready.
The bass riff. Now you play the bass riff; the band plays the stabs. Press start when you are ready.
Accompanying a singer. Support the voice, give the start, keep the beat, stay out of the way, and fit the style.
When you play for a singer, your job is to make them sound good. Play an introduction, keep a steady beat, and follow them if they slow down.
Keep your right hand below the singer's notes. Play less while they sing, and fill a little in the gaps. Simple and steady is best.
Choose a pattern for the style. A ballad has gentle broken chords. A waltz goes bass, chord, chord. Slow gospel rolls in groups of three.
Ballad under a voice. Left hand 1-5-8, right hand chords; the singer's tune plays above you. Press start when you are ready.
Waltz accompaniment. Bass on 1, chord on 2 and 3, under a tune. Press start when you are ready.
Gospel in twelve-eight. Four slow beats split in three, right-hand chords on each big beat, left hand rolling. Press start when you are ready.
Find your voice, match one note. Hear a note, sing it back, watch your pitch line land on the target.
Stand or sit tall, with loose shoulders. Breathe in low and quietly, like smelling a flower, so your tummy gently grows. Never push or strain your voice.
Listen to the note first. Hum it quietly inside your head. Then sing it on loo or ah. Deeper voices can sing it lower. The app accepts any octave.
While you sing, a line shows your pitch. Green means right on. Amber means close. Red means off. If you are too low, think up. If you are too high, relax.
Match C, E, G, D. Sing each note back and hold it steady. Press start when you are ready.
Do Re Mi, the first five notes. Sing up and down the first five notes of the major scale with solfège.
Do, re, mi, fa, sol are names for the steps of the scale. Do is home. Each one has its own feeling. Mi is bright. Sol is strong. Re wants to fall back to do.
All the steps here are small. Keep the sound smooth and connected, with one breath going up and one breath coming down.
Do to Sol and back no rush. Sing each step in turn. Press start when you are ready.
Do to Sol in time. Sing with the beat at 60 beats per minute. Press start when you are ready.
Leaps, thirds and fifths. Jump between Do, Mi and Sol accurately, the notes of the major chord.
Do to mi is a small jump. Do to sol is a bigger one. Before each jump, imagine the note in your head first, then sing it straight on, without sliding.
Do Mi Sol Mi Do. Leap cleanly to each note. Press start when you are ready.
Sight-sing a phrase. Read a short melody from the staff and sing it in time.
First find do. Look at the shape, steps or jumps, up or down. Tap the beat. Then sing. You can press Demo to hear it, but try once on your own first.
Phrase in time. Sing the phrase from the notation at 66 beats per minute. Press start when you are ready.

Listen to the chord. What kind of chord is it?

Four clicks, then a rhythm. Pick the words that fit, and say them out loud.
Listen to how fast it goes. Which tempo word fits?
Find the strong beat, then count to the next one. Which time signature is it?
Follow the signs like a road map. In what order do you play the bars?
Look at the note. Find a landmark note, count the steps, and pick its name.
